<reason>PRO built a clean symmetry case (same triangle, same statute, harder switching for workers, synergies laundering wage suppression) and then narrowed the debate decisively through its pressure questions. CON's opening conceded monopsony is real and that existing law already reaches it, leaving CON's live route as "evidence asymmetry + resource diversion + coin flip." PRO damaged each leg: "data follows attention" and the unanswered grocery-market rejoinder (delivery apps, warehouse clubs, Amazon) undercut the claim that labor markets are uniquely undefinable; the PRH case showed the tools in use; and "as seriously ≠ as confidently" plus "if the data fails, the claim loses and consumers lose nothing" neutralized the coin-flip framing. When pressed on what "proven" means, CON conceded the same preponderance standard, which PRO's closing turned into "same bar, but nobody checks." CON's fallback—that routine screening is a resourcing mandate on noisy evidence—is a real residual point and CON answered A1/A2 directly, but never showed why a filing-stage occupational-overlap screen is costly rather than cheap, and never rebutted the grocery messiness point. PRO's two clipped rebuttals are a genuine execution cost (losing the answer to CON's "direct fixes" line), keeping this competitive rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 [A3.1] forcing CON to define "proven," followed by CON's answer in [B4.1] that it is the ordinary preponderance/merger-specific standard; PRO's closing [A5.1]-[A5.5] then framed this as conceding the motion, reducing CON's position to "same bar, never tossed," with the "coin never tossed is the status quo" line landing memorably.</best_rebuttal>
